Arms build-up over time: three cartogram mockupsCountry size = major arms received over the previous 10 years (SIPRI TIV, military capability, not money). Colour = regime type that year. Drag the year or press Play: the change is smooth between years.

1Contiguous cartogram (like Worldmapper)

The whole map bends so each country's area matches its arms imports, and borders stay connected. Shapes are precomputed every 5 years in Python and morphed smoothly in between.

Pro: the most striking, the "wow" view; the world visibly reshapes around the Gulf, India, Egypt and Vietnam.
Con: shapes distort heavily, areas are about 6–16% off target, adds ~1.7 MB, and the 5-year keyframes miss short spikes.

2Scaled shapes in place

Every country keeps its real outline and grows or shrinks around its own centre. Area matches imports exactly. Countries may overlap or leave gaps.

Pro: exact areas, countries stay recognisable, smooth year by year, no extra data, cheap to build.
Con: big countries overlap their neighbours; less of a single "world reshaped" picture.

3Bubble cartogram

Each country becomes a circle with area equal to its imports, centred on the country's main landmass over a faint real map. Bubbles may shift at most a few pixels to avoid each other; a thin line points home when one is pushed. The largest are labelled.

Pro: the easiest to compare precisely, very smooth animation, labels fit.
Con: it looks least like a map; small countries become dots.
